query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the as‐built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA, prolonged exposure to elevated temperatures in either oxidizing or reducing environments promotes the diffusion‐driven nucleation and growth of Cr-rich sigma phase and nitride precipitates along grain boundaries. These secondary phases weaken intergranular cohesion and act as stress concentrators, which in turn trigger catastrophic failure through embrittlement.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built, supersaturated FCC matrix with fine, homogeneously dispersed constituents and minimal secondary phase precipitation.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled isothermal aging at elevated temperatures (approximately 950–1300 K) under well-defined oxidizing and reducing atmospheres.
generation.conditions: Temperatures in the range of about 950–1300 K for prolonged durations (e.g., >100 hours) with controlled gas compositions (oxidizing vs. reducing) to simulate service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain-boundary localized precipitates—specifically, Cr-rich sigma phase and nitride particles—that develop and coarsen during thermal exposure.
generation.mechanism: Elevated temperature enhances atomic diffusion that drives the formation and coarsening of brittle sigma and nitride precipitates particularly at grain boundaries. In oxidizing conditions, modified surface reactions may further accelerate these phase separations, whereas in reducing conditions similar diffusional kinetics prevail. The accumulation of these phases weakens the cohesive strength at interfaces, reducing ductility and toughness, and ultimately causing abrupt, catastrophic failure under applied stress.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-built state, aged specimens will show an increased volume fraction and size of grain boundary precipitates along with a corresponding drop in ductility and fracture toughness. The effect is expected to be more pronounced (or show different kinetics) between oxidizing and reducing environments, but in both cases leading to embrittlement and premature failure.
generation.baseline: The as-built HEA exhibits a single-phase, ductile FCC microstructure with high grain boundary cohesion and minimal secondary phase presence.
generation.boundary: Effects are anticipated within the temperature range of 950–1300 K and for exposure durations exceeding approximately 100 hours under controlled atmospheric conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The precise thresholds for precipitate volume fraction that lead to loss of mechanical integrity and the quantitative differences in degradation behavior between oxidizing and reducing environments remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of identical as-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA samples. Expose subsets of these samples isothermally at ~1000 K for 150 hours in two separate environments: one with a controlled oxidizing gas atmosphere and another with a reducing gas atmosphere. Retain an unaged control set. After exposure, conduct detailed microstructural characterization (using TEM, SEM, and XRD) to quantify the formation, size, and distribution of grain-boundary precipitates. Simultaneously, perform mechanical tests (microhardness and fracture toughness) to assess changes in ductility and intergranular cohesion.
measurements: Grain-boundary precipitate size and volume fraction (TEM/SEM analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If post-aging analyses show no statistically significant increase in grain-boundary precipitate formation or if the mechanical properties (ductility and fracture toughness) do not deteriorate relative to the as-built control—even under both oxidizing and reducing conditions—then the hypothesis that sigma phase/nitride precipitation at grain boundaries governs the degradation and catastrophic failure of the HEA will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The high entropy alloy (HEA) of equiatomic composition CrNiFeCoMn and with FCC crystal structure was additively manufactured in a selective laser melting (SLM) process starting from mechanically alloyed powders. The as-produced alloy shows fine nitride and σ phase precipitates, which are Cr-rich and stable up to about 900 K. The precipitates increase in number and dimensions after long-period annealing at 900–1300 K, with a change in the HEA mechanical properties. Higher aging temperatures in the furnace, above 1300 K, turn the alloy into a single FCC structure, with the disappearance of the nitride and σ phase precipitates inside the grains and at the grain boundaries, but still with the presence of a finer Cr-rich nitride precipitation phase. These results suggest that the as-produced HEA is a supersaturated solid solution at low and intermediate temperature with nitrides and σ nanostructures.

Whereas up to a certain working temperature fine precipitates can play a reinforcing role, starting from a temperature of about 950 K, the σ phase tends to swell and to preferentially place itself on the grain boundaries of the alloy. This in turn can lead to a significant reduction of the mechanical and chemical properties. This is described in the following and confirmed by a mechanical characterization with microhardness and hardness measurements that correlate with the microstructural evolution that occurs during aging.
Correlating with the microstructural and XRD investigations, these mechanical tests can provide important information on the stability and metastability of these high entropy alloys.
